client: I've been really struggling with going to this café near my office - it's where my ex and I used to meet all the time. Now every time I walk in, my heart starts pounding and I feel like I can't breathe properly. I know I should just avoid it, but it's the most convenient place to grab lunch, and part of me feels stupid for letting it affect me this much.
therapist:
It sounds like this café brings up some really strong physical reactions for you, which must feel quite overwhelming. I hear that conflict between wanting to avoid the discomfort but also not wanting to let it control your choices—that’s a tough spot to be in.  

What thoughts tend to run through your mind when you notice your heart start pounding in that space?

client:
When I feel my heart racing in that café, my mind immediately jumps to "Everyone can see how anxious I am" and "I'm going to embarrass myself." It's like my brain convinces me people are staring, even though logically I know they're probably not. The worst part is I used to love that place, and now I feel like my anxiety stole it from me. 

I tried pushing through it last week, but I had to leave after ten minutes because my hands were shaking so badly. Part of me wonders if I should just stop going altogether.
therapist:
It sounds like you're experiencing both the physical discomfort of anxiety and the frustration of losing a place that once brought you joy. Those thoughts about being judged can feel so convincing in the moment, even when we know they might not be accurate.

What do you think might happen if you experimented with observing those "people are staring" thoughts as just passing mental events, rather than facts?

client:
I get what you're saying about observing the thoughts instead of believing them, but it's not that easy. When I'm in the moment at the coffee shop, my whole body is screaming that people are judging me. It feels so real. 

I've tried noticing the thoughts before, but they just take over anyway. What if people actually are staring and thinking bad things about me? That possibility makes it even harder to just observe the thoughts calmly.
therapist:
I hear how real and overwhelming those physical sensations feel in the moment—when your body is reacting so strongly, it can make those anxious thoughts feel undeniably true. That "what if" about people actually judging you adds another layer of distress, doesn't it?

When you've tried noticing the thoughts before, what typically happens right before they take over completely? (That moment might hold some useful clues.)

client:
I start noticing my chest getting tight and my breathing getting shallow right before the thoughts spiral. It's like my body is sounding an alarm before my mind even catches up. But when I try to notice it, I just get more scared because it feels like proof that something bad is really happening. 

I don't know if focusing on those moments helps - sometimes it just makes me more aware of how anxious I am. Like I'm watching myself fall apart instead of stopping it.
therapist:
It makes complete sense that noticing those physical symptoms would feel like confirmation that danger is real—your body's alarm system is working overtime here. That experience of watching yourself get anxious without being able to stop it can feel so discouraging.  

What if we shifted focus slightly—instead of trying to stop the anxiety or judge whether it's "proof" of danger, could we practice simply naming what's happening in those early moments? Like softly noting "tight chest" or "shallow breath," almost like a weather report?

client:
I get what you're saying about naming the symptoms instead of fighting them, but when my chest gets tight like that, it's hard to just observe it calmly. It feels like the start of something really bad, and my brain immediately jumps to worst-case scenarios. 

I've tried mindfulness stuff before and it just made me more frustrated because the anxiety didn't go away - it felt like I was just sitting there letting myself suffer. How is noticing my shallow breathing supposed to help when it still feels like I can't get enough air?
therapist:
It sounds like that moment when your chest tightens triggers such a strong sense of impending danger that simply observing it feels impossible—like trying to watch a storm when you're already being swept away by it. That frustration when mindfulness doesn't "fix" the anxiety right away is completely understandable—our brains often want solutions, not observation.  

What if we explored this differently: when you notice that first tightness, could you experiment with pairing the observation with one grounding action—like pressing your feet firmly into the floor—to give your brain something concrete to do alongside the noticing?

client: I get what you're saying about the grounding action, but when my chest tightens it feels like my whole body locks up. Pressing my feet down sounds simple, but in the moment I'm so focused on the panic that I can't even remember to do it. It's frustrating because I know these techniques are supposed to help, but they feel impossible when I actually need them.
therapist:
That frustration makes so much sense—when panic takes over, even simple actions can feel completely out of reach, which can make the whole situation feel even more hopeless. It might help to remember that skills often feel impossible *until* we've practiced them repeatedly in calmer moments first—like training muscles before running a race.  

Could we try something? Pick one non-panic time this week to *pretend* your chest is tightening, and practice pressing your feet down then—just to build the association when there’s no real pressure?

client:
I don't know... the idea of intentionally making myself uncomfortable even when I'm not panicking sounds counterintuitive. What if triggering those physical sensations just makes me start actually panicking? I've had that happen before when I tried similar exercises. 

Part of me gets what you're saying about practicing before the real thing, but another part worries this could backfire. My anxiety feels so fragile - like any little nudge could send me spiraling.
therapist:
I hear how scary that possibility feels—like walking too close to the edge of a spiral you've experienced before. That fear of accidentally tipping yourself into panic makes complete sense, especially when anxiety has felt so unpredictable in the past.  

What if we started even smaller—not with intentionally creating discomfort, but just noticing the *natural* rise and fall of your breath right now, with zero pressure to change it? That way, we're building observation skills without triggering the alarm. How does that land for you?

client:
I get what you're saying about just noticing my breath, but honestly even that makes me nervous. What if focusing on it makes me hyperventilate or something? Last time I tried paying attention to my breathing during a yoga class, I started feeling lightheaded and had to leave. 

I do like the idea of starting small though. It's just... I don't trust my own body's reactions anymore. Everything feels like it could spiral out of control so easily.
therapist:
It sounds like even small steps toward observing your body bring up understandable wariness—that experience in yoga class must have felt really unsettling when you were just trying something meant to be calming. That loss of trust in your own physical responses makes this work feel especially delicate, doesn't it?  

What if we shifted focus to something outside your body entirely for now—maybe noticing five colors in the room whenever you feel wary? That way, we're building observation skills without immediately confronting the sensations that feel most risky.

client:
I see what you're saying about focusing on colors instead of body sensations, but even that feels like too much right now. When I try to pay attention to my surroundings, my mind just keeps going back to how shaky and out of control I felt during yoga. 

I guess part of me worries that any kind of noticing exercise will just remind me of that awful experience. It's like my brain keeps replaying that moment when my heart started racing for no reason.
therapist:
It makes complete sense that even external focus feels too charged right now—that yoga experience really left a deep mark, and your brain is understandably protective against anything that might remind you of that loss of control.  

Could we try something completely different? Instead of focusing on sensations or surroundings, what if we simply named one safe thing in this exact moment—like the fact that you're sitting in a stable chair or that the lights are on? No pressure, just naming what's already true and unchanging.

client: That actually sounds... okay, I guess. The chair thing is kind of obvious, but I can feel the solidness of it under me. It's just... I don't know if this will help long-term. My mind keeps jumping to how I froze up in that yoga class last week, and now even simple things feel threatening. What if naming safe things just becomes another thing I fail at?
therapist:
I hear that mix of tentative openness and lingering doubt—the chair feels solid right now, but there's still that fear that even this small step might not work or could become another source of disappointment. That worry about "failing" at coping skills adds such a heavy weight to trying anything new.  

What if we treated this purely as information-gathering for now—no success or failure, just noticing what happens when you name one safe thing, even if your mind immediately protests? Like a scientist calmly taking notes, without needing the experiment to "work"?
